PSE II · Chapter 25

Capacitance & Dielectrics

Storing charge, storing energy

← PSE II Course

25.0 — Storing the Electric Field

Chapters 22 through 24 built a complete framework for electrostatics. Charges create fields (Ch 22). Gauss’s Law relates a field to the charge enclosed (Ch 23). Potential turns the vector field into a scalar landscape, and the energy of a configuration turns out to reside in the field itself, at a density \(u_E = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\) (Ch 24).

That framework was descriptive: given charges, find the field. This chapter asks the engineering question in the other direction. Can we build a device that deliberately creates a field, and stores the energy in it?

The answer is the capacitor, and the physics reduces to one idea: two conductors separated by a gap, carrying equal and opposite charge. From that single arrangement come camera flashes, defibrillators, the smoothing in every power supply, and the touchscreen this may be displayed on.

This chapter was already opened at the end of Chapter 24. Working the coaxial cable in §24.6 produced

\[\Delta V = \frac{2k_eQ}{\ell}\ln\!\left(\frac{b}{a}\right) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{Q}{\Delta V} = \frac{\ell}{2k_e\ln(b/a)}\]

and the right-hand side contains only lengths — no charge, no voltage. Double \(Q\) and \(\Delta V\) doubles with it, leaving the ratio untouched. A fixed number, set by geometry alone, saying how much charge the pair holds per volt.

That number is what this chapter is about. Chapter 24 found it; Chapter 25 names it, computes it for the geometries that matter, and asks what it costs to fill.

The earliest capacitor — the Leyden jar — was invented independently in 1745 by Ewald Georg von Kleist (1700–1748) and Pieter van Musschenbroek (1692–1761) in Leiden. A glass jar coated inside and out with metal foil; its capacity to store a shock astonished everyone who touched one.

“I would like to tell you about a new but terrible experiment, which I advise you never to try yourself… I felt myself struck in my arms, shoulders, and breast so that I lost my breath, and it was two days before I recovered from the effects of the blow and the terror.” — Pieter van Musschenbroek, 1746

Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) later established that the charge sat not in the water inside the jar but on the glass surfaces — moving attention to the geometry of the conductors and the material between them. Those are exactly the two things capacitance depends on.

*Capacitance is where field theory becomes circuit theory. Gauss’s Law gives the field, integration gives the potential, and the ratio of charge to potential is a number you can print on a component and solder into a board.

25.1 — Definition of Capacitance

A capacitor is two conductors — its plates — carrying charges of equal magnitude and opposite sign. When we say a capacitor “holds charge \(Q\),” we mean one plate carries \(+Q\) and the other \(-Q\). The net charge is zero. What is stored is the separation of charge, and the field that separation creates.

The Definition

\[\boxed{\;C \equiv \frac{Q}{\Delta V}\;} \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad Q = C\,\Delta V\]

Here \(Q\) is the magnitude of the charge on either plate, \(\Delta V\) the magnitude of the potential difference between them, and \(C\) the capacitance. The unit is the farad (F), after Michael Faraday: \(1\ \text{F} = 1\ \text{C/V}\).

Capacitance depends only on geometry and on the material between the plates — never on \(Q\) or \(\Delta V\). That is not an approximation; it follows from the definition. Every capacitance formula in this chapter will be built by assuming a charge \(Q\), computing the \(\Delta V\) it produces, and dividing — and \(Q\) will cancel every single time.

Why the ratio is the useful quantity. Put twice the charge on a capacitor and the field everywhere doubles, so \(\Delta V\) doubles too. The ratio does not move. That is what makes \(C\) a property of the device rather than of its present state — you can stamp it on the component before knowing what circuit it will sit in.

A Farad Is Enormous

Practical capacitors are measured in picofarads (\(10^{-12}\) F), nanofarads (\(10^{-9}\) F), or microfarads (\(10^{-6}\) F). A one-farad capacitor charged to one volt has separated \(6.24\times10^{18}\) electrons. The supercapacitors in hybrid vehicles reach thousands of farads and are a genuine engineering achievement; §25.3 will show that even the Earth, treated as an isolated conductor, comes in under a millifarad.

*Students routinely confuse capacitance with charge. A large capacitance means a lot of charge per volt. A swimming pool and a drinking glass can both be full; the pool holds far more water per inch of depth.

25.2 — Calculating Capacitance: The Parallel-Plate Capacitor

The General Strategy

Every capacitance calculation in this chapter follows four steps, and they are the tools of the last two chapters used in sequence:

  1. Assume charges \(\pm Q\) on the two conductors.
  2. Find \(\vec E\) between them, using Gauss’s Law (Ch 23).
  3. Integrate for the potential difference, \(\Delta V = -\int\vec E\cdot d\vec s\) (Ch 24).
  4. Divide: \(C = Q/\Delta V\).

Steps 2 and 3 are not new work. They are precisely the two routes of Chapter 24 — Gauss’s Law for the field, then Route 2 to integrate it. Chapter 25 adds only step 4, and step 4 is a division. The whole of this chapter’s machinery was assembled last chapter; what is new is the interpretation of the result as a property of a manufactured object.

The Parallel-Plate Capacitor

Two parallel conducting plates, each of area \(A\), separated by \(d\), with \(d\) small enough that the field between them is uniform and edge effects are negligible.

Step 1 — assume the charge. Surface charge density \(\sigma = Q/A\).

Step 2 — the field. Ch 23’s pillbox result for a conducting surface gives a uniform field between the plates:

\[E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0 A}\]

Step 3 — the potential difference. The field is uniform and the path is along it, so the integral is trivial:

\[\Delta V = Ed = \frac{Qd}{\varepsilon_0 A}\]

Step 4 — divide. The \(Q\) cancels, as promised:

\[\boxed{\;C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\;}\]

Check the limits, and read the physics off them.

  • Larger \(A\) \(\Rightarrow\) larger \(C\). More plate area is more room to park charge at a given voltage.
  • Smaller \(d\) \(\Rightarrow\) larger \(C\). Bring the plates closer and each plate’s field holds the opposite charge more tightly, so more charge sits there for the same \(\Delta V\).
  • \(d \to 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(C \to \infty\). Correct in the idealisation, and the reason it does not happen in practice is §25.6: every real insulator breaks down at a finite field.
  • Nothing about \(Q\) or \(\Delta V\) survives — the promise of §25.1, kept.

A Typical Parallel-Plate Capacitor

Square plates \(10.0\) cm on a side, separated by \(d = 1.00\) mm. Find \(C\).

\[C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = \frac{(8.854\times10^{-12})(0.100)^2}{1.00\times10^{-3}}\]

\[\boxed{\;C = 88.5\ \text{pF}\;}\]

That number is worth pausing on. Plates the size of a coffee-table book, held a millimetre apart, give 88.5 picofarads — about one ten-billionth of a farad. Every practical capacitor therefore does two things this one does not: it fills the gap with a dielectric (§25.6), which multiplies \(C\) by a factor of a few to a few hundred, and it rolls the plates up so that a large area occupies a small volume.

25.3 — Capacitance of Other Geometries

The same four steps work wherever the symmetry is good enough for Gauss’s Law. Both of the cases below were already worked in Chapters 23 and 24 — Gauss’s Law supplied the field, and §24.6 integrated it. Only step 4 is new.

The Cylindrical Capacitor

An inner conductor of radius \(a\) inside a coaxial shell of radius \(b\), both of length \(\ell\). This is every coaxial cable ever made.

From §24.6, \(\Delta V = 2k_e\lambda\ln(b/a)\) with \(\lambda = Q/\ell\). Divide:

\[\boxed{\;C = \frac{\ell}{2k_e\ln(b/a)}\;} \qquad\text{or per unit length}\qquad \frac{C}{\ell} = \frac{2\pi\varepsilon_0}{\ln(b/a)}\]

The Spherical Capacitor

An inner sphere of radius \(a\) inside a concentric shell of radius \(b\).

From §24.6, \(\Delta V = k_eQ\left(\tfrac1a - \tfrac1b\right)\). Divide:

\[\boxed{\;C = \frac{ab}{k_e(b-a)}\;}\]

The limit that matters: let the outer conductor go away. Take \(b\to\infty\) in the spherical result. Write it as \(C = a/[k_e(1 - a/b)]\); as \(b\to\infty\) the correction dies and

\[C \;\longrightarrow\; \frac{a}{k_e} = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 a\]

A single isolated sphere has a capacitance, with no second conductor in sight. That is not a trick — the “other plate” is infinity, where the potential is zero, and the sphere still holds a definite charge per volt.

Put the Earth in: \(a = 6.37\times10^6\) m gives \(C = 710\ \mu\)F. A planet comes in under a millifarad. It is the sharpest possible statement of how large the farad is.

Note also that the cylindrical result has no such limit — \(\ln(b/a)\) diverges as \(b\to\infty\), so \(C\to 0\). An infinite line has no finite capacitance to infinity, for the same reason it had no finite potential there (§24.6).

Geometry Capacitance Set by
Parallel plate \(C = \varepsilon_0 A/d\) area \(A\), separation \(d\)
Cylindrical \(C = \ell/[2k_e\ln(b/a)]\) length \(\ell\), radii \(a\), \(b\)
Spherical \(C = ab/[k_e(b-a)]\) radii \(a\), \(b\)
Isolated sphere \(C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 a\) radius \(a\)

In every row: geometry and \(\varepsilon_0\), nothing else.

25.4 — Combinations of Capacitors

Real circuits combine capacitors to reach values and voltage ratings that no single component provides. Two questions settle every combination: which quantity is shared, and which one adds.

Parallel Combination

Capacitors are in parallel when the same \(\Delta V\) appears across each. Both top plates connect to one node, both bottom plates to another, so each capacitor sees the same two potentials.

Shared \(\Delta V\); the charges add:

\[Q_{\text{tot}} = Q_1 + Q_2 = C_1\Delta V + C_2\Delta V = (C_1 + C_2)\Delta V\]

\[\boxed{\;C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2 + C_3 + \cdots \qquad (\text{parallel})\;}\]

Parallel capacitors behave as one capacitor with more plate area. \(C_{\text{eq}}\) is always larger than the largest capacitor in the group.

Series Combination

Capacitors are in series when connected end to end, so that the same charge \(Q\) appears on each.

Why series capacitors must carry equal charge, and it is not an assumption. The conductor between two series capacitors — the bottom plate of the first joined to the top plate of the second — is electrically isolated. No wire reaches it from the battery. Whatever charge the battery pushes onto the first capacitor’s top plate induces an equal and opposite charge on the plate facing it, and the charge displaced from that plate has nowhere to go but the next capacitor. The isolated middle conductor started neutral and must stay neutral, which forces \(Q\) to be identical all the way along.

Shared \(Q\); the voltages add:

\[\Delta V_{\text{tot}} = \Delta V_1 + \Delta V_2 = \frac{Q}{C_1} + \frac{Q}{C_2} = Q\left(\frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2}\right)\]

\[\boxed{\;\frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \frac{1}{C_3} + \cdots \qquad (\text{series})\;}\]

Series capacitors behave as one capacitor with a larger plate separation. \(C_{\text{eq}}\) is always smaller than the smallest capacitor in the group.

Series and Parallel at a Glance

Property Parallel Series
Shared quantity \(\Delta V\) \(Q\)
Additive quantity \(Q_{\text{tot}} = Q_1 + Q_2\) \(\Delta V_{\text{tot}} = \Delta V_1 + \Delta V_2\)
Combination rule \(C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2\) \(1/C_{\text{eq}} = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2\)
Effect larger than any one smaller than any one
Physical picture more area more separation

These are the spring rules from Physics I, not the resistor rules. Springs in parallel share a displacement and their stiffnesses add, \(k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 + k_2\) — exactly the parallel-capacitor rule. Springs in series share a force and their compliances add, \(1/k_{\text{eq}} = 1/k_1 + 1/k_2\) — exactly the series-capacitor rule.

The correspondence runs \(C \leftrightarrow k\), \(\Delta V \leftrightarrow x\), \(Q \leftrightarrow F\), and §25.5 will show it extends to the stored energy.

Resistors, in Chapter 27, combine the opposite way — series resistances add. That reversal catches people every term, and the reason is worth carrying: it is \(C\) that adds in parallel because \(C\) measures capacity, while \(R\) measures opposition.

A Mixed Combination

\(C_1 = 4.00\ \mu\)F and \(C_2 = 6.00\ \mu\)F in series; that pair in parallel with \(C_4 = 8.00\ \mu\)F; the whole group in series with \(C_3 = 2.00\ \mu\)F, across \(\Delta V = 12.0\) V.

Work from the inside out. There is no formula for a network; there is only repeated application of the two rules to the innermost group that is purely series or purely parallel.

Step 1 — \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) in series:

\[\frac{1}{C_{12}} = \frac{1}{4.00} + \frac{1}{6.00} = \frac{5}{12} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad C_{12} = 2.40\ \mu\text{F}\]

Step 2 — that pair in parallel with \(C_4\):

\[C_{124} = C_{12} + C_4 = 2.40 + 8.00 = 10.4\ \mu\text{F}\]

Step 3 — the group in series with \(C_3\):

\[\frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{10.4} + \frac{1}{2.00} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad C_{\text{eq}} = 1.68\ \mu\text{F}\]

\[\boxed{\;C_{\text{eq}} = 1.68\ \mu\text{F}\;}\]

Check it against the bounds before trusting it. The last operation was a series combination with \(C_3 = 2.00\ \mu\)F, so the answer must come out smaller than \(2.00\ \mu\)F — and \(1.68\) is. Step 2 was a parallel combination, so \(10.4\) had to exceed \(8.00\) — it does. Step 1 was series, so \(2.40\) had to fall below \(4.00\) — it does.

Every step of a network reduction has a one-line sanity check available. Using them catches the single most common error in this material: applying the series rule to a parallel pair, or the reverse.

25.5 — Energy Stored in a Charged Capacitor

Charging a capacitor is not free, and the reason is that it gets harder as you go. Move the first \(dq\) across and the plates are still neutral — no field, no opposition. But every charge delivered raises the potential difference, so the next one costs more.

At the moment the capacitor holds charge \(q\), the potential difference is \(q/C\), and moving one more increment costs

\[dW = \Delta V\,dq = \frac{q}{C}\,dq\]

Integrate from empty to full:

\[U = \int_0^Q \frac{q}{C}\,dq = \frac{1}{C}\left[\frac{q^2}{2}\right]_0^Q = \frac{Q^2}{2C}\]

\[\boxed{\;U = \frac{Q^2}{2C} = \frac{1}{2}C(\Delta V)^2 = \frac{1}{2}Q\,\Delta V\;}\]

All three forms are the same statement, converted between by \(Q = C\Delta V\). In practice: use \(\tfrac12 C(\Delta V)^2\) when the battery stays connected and holds the voltage; use \(Q^2/2C\) when the battery has been disconnected and the charge is what is fixed.

Where the factor of one half comes from. The final charge \(Q\) sits at the final voltage \(\Delta V\), so a first guess of \(Q\Delta V\) is natural — and wrong by a factor of two. Only the last increment of charge paid full voltage; the first paid nothing, and the average over the whole process was \(\Delta V/2\).

The figure says the same thing geometrically: \(\Delta V = q/C\) is a straight line through the origin, so the work — the area beneath it — is a triangle, and a triangle is half the enclosing rectangle.

A capacitor is the electrical analogue of a spring.

Spring (Physics I) Capacitor (here)
\(U = \tfrac12 kx^2\) \(U = \tfrac12 C(\Delta V)^2\)
stiffness \(k\) capacitance \(C\)
displacement \(x\) voltage \(\Delta V\)
\(F = kx\) \(Q = C\Delta V\)

Energy quadratic in the “displacement,” force linear in it, and — as §25.4 showed — the same series and parallel combination rules. It is the same mathematical object wearing different units.

Energy in a Defibrillator

A defibrillator stores energy in a \(C = 32.0\ \mu\)F capacitor charged to \(5000\) V.

\[U = \tfrac12 C(\Delta V)^2 = \tfrac12 (32.0\times10^{-6})(5000)^2\]

\[\boxed{\;U = 400\ \text{J}\;}\]

Why a capacitor and not a battery. \(400\) J is modest — a few seconds of a household light bulb. What matters is that a capacitor can deliver it in milliseconds, which is a power of order \(10^5\) W. A battery stores far more total energy and cannot release it anywhere near that fast. Capacitors are not about how much energy; they are about how quickly.

Energy Density: The Field Holds the Energy

Where is the energy? Not “on the plates” — in the field between them. Take the parallel-plate case, whose field fills a volume \(Ad\), and substitute \(C = \varepsilon_0A/d\) and \(\Delta V = Ed\):

\[U = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\right)(Ed)^2 = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2 (Ad)\]

The bracket \((Ad)\) is exactly the volume occupied by the field, so the energy per unit volume is

\[\boxed{\;u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\;}\]

Derived from one geometry, true in all of them. Nothing in the final expression remembers plates, area, or separation — only the local field strength. That is the signature of a genuinely local statement: wherever there is an electric field, there is energy at this density, whether or not any capacitor is nearby.

This is the same \(u_E\) met in Chapter 24, arrived at from the opposite direction. There it came from the work of assembling charge; here from the work of charging a device. Two routes, one number.

*This result is the seed of a much larger idea. If energy lives in the field, then a field that detaches from its source carries energy away with it — which is what an electromagnetic wave is, and what Chapter 30 is about.

25.6 — Capacitors with Dielectrics

In 1837 Michael Faraday found that sliding a nonconducting material — a dielectric — into the gap increases the capacitance. The experiment is worth stating precisely, because the bookkeeping depends on how it is done.

Charge a capacitor to \(\Delta V_0\), disconnect the battery so that \(Q\) is fixed, then insert the dielectric. The voltage falls, to \(\Delta V_0/\kappa\), where \(\kappa \ge 1\) is the dielectric constant of the material. Since \(Q\) did not change and \(\Delta V\) fell by \(\kappa\):

\[\boxed{\;C = \kappa C_0\;} \qquad\text{and for parallel plates}\qquad \boxed{\;C = \frac{\kappa\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\;}\]

Material \(\kappa\) Dielectric strength (\(10^6\) V/m)
Vacuum 1.00000 —
Air 1.00059 3
Teflon 2.1 60
Paper 3.7 16
Glass (Pyrex) 5.6 14
Water 80 —
Strontium titanate 233 8

Why a Dielectric Increases Capacitance

The mechanism is polarization. Place an insulator in a field and its charge cannot flow — but it can shift.

  • Polar molecules already carry a permanent dipole moment. The field exerts a torque that rotates them into alignment.
  • Nonpolar molecules have no permanent dipole, but the field pulls their electron clouds one way and nuclei the other, inducing one.

Either way the material ends up with aligned dipoles: a layer of negative charge facing the positive plate, positive facing the negative plate. Those surface layers produce a field opposing the original, so the net field drops:

\[E = \frac{E_0}{\kappa}\]

A weaker field means a smaller \(\Delta V\) across the same gap, and a smaller \(\Delta V\) for the same \(Q\) means a larger \(C\). It is convenient to fold \(\kappa\) into a permittivity \(\varepsilon = \kappa\varepsilon_0\), so that \(C = \varepsilon A/d\) and the vacuum case is just \(\kappa = 1\).

Two Scenarios, and They Differ

Everything depends on whether the battery is still attached.

Quantity Battery connected (\(\Delta V\) fixed) Battery disconnected (\(Q\) fixed)
Capacitance \(C\) \(\times\kappa\) \(\times\kappa\)
Charge \(Q\) \(\times\kappa\) unchanged
Voltage \(\Delta V\) unchanged \(\div\kappa\)
Energy \(U\) \(\times\kappa\) \(\div\kappa\)

The energy column is the one to think about, because it moves in opposite directions.

Battery connected: \(U = \tfrac12 C(\Delta V)^2\) with \(\Delta V\) held fixed and \(C\) up by \(\kappa\), so \(U\) rises. The battery supplied the extra energy — it pushed additional charge onto the plates to maintain the voltage.

Battery disconnected: \(U = Q^2/2C\) with \(Q\) held fixed and \(C\) up by \(\kappa\), so \(U\) falls. Nothing is missing: the capacitor did work on the dielectric. The fringing field at the edge of the gap pulls the slab inward, and the energy lost from the field went into that mechanical work. Let go of a dielectric slab near a charged capacitor and it is drawn in — that is the same energy, visible.

Dielectric Strength and Breakdown

Every insulator fails at a large enough field. Beyond its dielectric strength, the material ionises and suddenly conducts — a spark, an arc, or on the largest scale, lightning. The maximum voltage a capacitor can hold is

\[\Delta V_{\text{max}} = E_{\text{max}}\,d\]

A dielectric earns its place twice over. It multiplies \(C\) by \(\kappa\), and because its dielectric strength usually exceeds air’s \(3\times10^6\) V/m, it also raises \(\Delta V_{\text{max}}\). Teflon does both aggressively: \(\kappa = 2.1\) with a strength of \(60\times10^6\) V/m, twenty times air’s.

This is also why \(d \to 0\) does not really give \(C \to \infty\) (§25.2). Shrinking the gap raises the field at fixed voltage, and the material breaks down first.

Partially Filled Gaps

A slab that fills only part of the gap is not a special case needing new physics — it is two capacitors, and §25.4 already says how to combine them. The only question is which rule applies, and the answer is decided by how the slab is placed.

Stacked (one above the other). Each layer spans the full plate area \(A\) but only part of the separation. They share the same charge, so they are in series:

\[C_i = \frac{\kappa_i\varepsilon_0 A}{d_i}, \qquad \frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2}\]

Side by side (each covering part of the area). Each slab spans the full separation \(d\) but only part of the area. They share the same voltage, so they are in parallel:

\[C_i = \frac{\kappa_i\varepsilon_0 A_i}{d}, \qquad C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2\]

The stacked case is the dangerous one, and the figure shows why. With \(\kappa = 4.0\) filling the lower half, the two layers carry the same charge, so the smaller capacitance takes the larger share of the voltage — and the air layer, with \(\kappa = 1\), is the smaller one. It absorbs \(80\) of the \(100\) V across half the gap, giving it four times the field inside the slab.

So the air breaks down first, at a total voltage well below what the dielectric alone could withstand. A gap that is partly air is limited by the air, which is why capacitors are built with the dielectric filling the gap completely and why a trapped bubble is a manufacturing defect rather than a cosmetic one.

Side by side, nothing of the sort happens: both halves see the same \(\Delta V\) across the same \(d\), so both see the same field, and the one with the larger \(\kappa\) simply stores proportionally more charge.

Inserting a Dielectric

\(C_0 = 100\) pF is charged to \(\Delta V_0 = 50.0\) V. The battery is then disconnected, and a slab with \(\kappa = 5.0\) is inserted.

Before insertion, the charge is fixed at

\[Q = C_0\Delta V_0 = (100\times10^{-12})(50.0) = 5.00\ \text{nC}\]

(a) The new capacitance. \(C = \kappa C_0 = 5.0(100) = 500\) pF.

(b) The new voltage. \(Q\) is unchanged, so

\[\Delta V = \frac{Q}{C} = \frac{5.00\times10^{-9}}{500\times10^{-12}} = 10.0\ \text{V}\]

(c) The energies.

\[U_0 = \frac{Q^2}{2C_0} = 125\ \text{nJ}, \qquad U = \frac{Q^2}{2C} = 25.0\ \text{nJ}\]

\[\boxed{\;C = 500\ \text{pF}, \qquad \Delta V = 10.0\ \text{V}, \qquad \frac{U}{U_0} = \frac{1}{\kappa} = \frac{1}{5}\;}\]

The voltage fell by exactly \(\kappa\) and the energy by exactly \(\kappa\), both as the table predicts. The missing \(100\) nJ is not lost — it is the work the fringing field did pulling the slab into the gap. Had the battery stayed connected instead, every entry in this example would differ, and the energy would have gone up by a factor of five.

Electric Dipoles in a Field

The polarization argument rests on dipoles turning, so it is worth writing down what a field does to one. For a dipole \(\vec p = q\vec d\) in a uniform field, the two forces are equal and opposite — no net force — but they act at different points, so they produce a torque:

\[\boxed{\;\vec\tau = \vec p \times \vec E \qquad\qquad U = -\vec p\cdot\vec E = -pE\cos\theta\;}\]

The energy is minimum when \(\vec p\) is parallel to \(\vec E\) — the stable alignment — and maximum when antiparallel. In a non-uniform field the two forces no longer cancel, and the dipole is pulled toward the stronger field. That is the force that drags a dielectric slab into a capacitor gap.

These two expressions return almost unchanged for magnetic dipoles in Chapter 28: \(\vec\tau = \vec\mu\times\vec B\) and \(U = -\vec\mu\cdot\vec B\). Same mathematics, different letters — worth noticing now so that it costs nothing later.

25.7 — Applications of Capacitors

Energy storage and fast release. Camera flashes, defibrillators, pulsed lasers, and the capacitor banks that drive particle accelerators all exploit the same property: modest stored energy, delivered in microseconds to milliseconds.

Capacitive sensing. Since \(C = \kappa\varepsilon_0A/d\), anything that changes \(d\), \(A\), or \(\kappa\) changes \(C\) measurably:

  • a keyboard key presses one plate closer, reducing \(d\);
  • a touchscreen registers a finger because tissue alters the local \(\kappa\);
  • an accelerometer lets a small proof mass move a plate;
  • a humidity sensor works because water’s \(\kappa \approx 80\) dwarfs air’s.

Filtering and timing. Capacitors smooth the pulsating output of a rectifier into usable DC, and paired with a resistor they set a time constant \(\tau = RC\) — the basis of every timing circuit. RC circuits are Chapter 27.

25.8 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. Capacitance \(C = Q/\Delta V\) is the charge stored per volt. It depends only on geometry and the dielectric, never on \(Q\) or \(\Delta V\). Unit: the farad, which is enormous.
  2. Every capacitance is computed the same way: assume \(\pm Q\), get \(\vec E\) from Gauss’s Law, integrate for \(\Delta V\), divide. The \(Q\) always cancels.
  3. Parallel plates give \(C = \varepsilon_0A/d\); cylindrical and spherical geometries follow from Chapter 24’s integrals. An isolated sphere has \(C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 a\) — no second conductor required.
  4. Parallel: shared \(\Delta V\), charges add, \(C_{\text{eq}} = \sum C_i\). Series: shared \(Q\), voltages add, \(1/C_{\text{eq}} = \sum 1/C_i\). These are the spring rules, not the resistor rules.
  5. Stored energy \(U = Q^2/2C = \tfrac12 C(\Delta V)^2\). The factor of \(\tfrac12\) is because the average charging voltage is half the final one.
  6. The energy is in the field, at density \(u_E = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\) — the same result Chapter 24 reached from assembling charge.
  7. A dielectric multiplies \(C\) by \(\kappa\) through polarization, and raises the breakdown voltage. Whether \(U\) rises or falls depends entirely on whether the battery is still connected.

Key Equations

Quantity Equation
Capacitance \(C = Q/\Delta V\)
Parallel plate \(C = \varepsilon_0 A/d\)
Cylindrical \(C = \ell/[2k_e\ln(b/a)]\)
Spherical \(C = ab/[k_e(b-a)]\)
Isolated sphere \(C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 a\)
Parallel combination \(C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots\)
Series combination \(1/C_{\text{eq}} = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 + \cdots\)
Stored energy \(U = Q^2/2C = \tfrac12C(\Delta V)^2 = \tfrac12Q\Delta V\)
Energy density \(u_E = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\)
With dielectric \(C = \kappa\varepsilon_0A/d\)
Breakdown \(\Delta V_{\text{max}} = E_{\text{max}}d\)
Dipole in a field \(\vec\tau = \vec p\times\vec E\); \(U = -\vec p\cdot\vec E\)

Looking Ahead

Chapter 26 sets the charges moving. Current, resistance, and Ohm’s Law (\(\Delta V = IR\)) arrive, and resistance will turn out to depend on material and geometry much as capacitance does — though it combines by the opposite rules.

Capacitors then return in Chapter 27, paired with resistors, where the stored energy drains through a resistance on a timescale \(\tau = RC\).

*Chapters 22–25 form one arc: charge, to force, to field, to potential, to stored energy. Everything so far has been static. From Chapter 26 the charges move, and almost everything you will build is on the other side of that line.
